sections.html:
Cash to a buyer who takes the house as it stands is the quickest way out in Trenton, since that buyer deals with the city's transfer paperwork. An agent listing can suit a house in good shape, and you may sell without an agent, yet all three routes go through the same city inspection before the deed moves.

Trenton is the state capital and the Mercer County seat, with an estimated 91,506 residents in mid-2025 on 7.58 square miles of land. Houses sit tightly packed, and many are older rowhouses.

sections.h2: What Trenton homes cost and who owns them
sections.html:
The middle value of an owner-occupied home is $160,700 and median gross rent is $1,294. Only 37.9 percent of the city's 32,052 households own the home they live in, and median household income is $52,537. Many sellers are therefore landlords, heirs or owners of older houses that need work.

Owner costs median $1,717 a month with a mortgage and $752 without, so holding a paid-off house is cheap. That helps explain why inherited houses can sit a long while before anyone decides to sell.

Trenton requires a Certificate of Housing Code Compliance before the change of ownership of any residential property. The Division of Housing Inspections issues it after confirming zoning and fire-safety compliance, working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, and substantial conformity with the city's habitability standards.

The seller or the seller's agent files the application, because the buyer has no legal right to enter the property before the sale. A buyer who has agreed to obtain the certificate may file instead. After the inspection the city hands over a list of violations, and the certificate is issued once they are corrected. A Certificate of Approval or a Certificate of Continued Occupancy can stand in for it. Commercial transfers need no inspection unless the structure contains a residential unit.

If the house cannot pass, the owner can file an affidavit with the Department of Inspections stating the property will stay unoccupied until a certificate is obtained. That is the usual path for a cash buyer who plans a full renovation.

Trenton inspection fees and rules
Inspection itemRule or fee
Certificate of Housing Code Compliance$200, plus $15 per unit above four units
Re-inspection, 1 or 2 units$50 each time after the first
Re-inspection, 3 or more units$25 per unit
How long the certificate lastsSix months
Unoccupied-until-certified affidavitAllowed in place of the certificate at transfer
Yearly landlord license, residential$90 per structure plus $25 per unit

Trenton runs an Absentee Owner Program that requires every owner of rented residential or commercial property to hold a license, renewed each January. A single-family rental carries a $115 minimum fee. If you sell a tenant-occupied building, confirm the license is current, because a lapse can complicate the transfer.

Rental units also need their own inspection before a tenant moves in. The city no longer issues stickers, so a tenant or buyer calls to confirm a current rental certificate. Vacant structures face the steepest charge: a flat $500 registration fee, then $1,300 on the first renewal, $2,000 on the second and $3,000 after that.

  • A house that sits empty for a year or more costs its owner real money in registration fees.
  • Owners of vacant land and vacant buildings answer to the same Division of Housing Inspections.
  • Sidewalk damage from tree roots goes to the division's sidewalk inspection section, so check it before a buyer's walkthrough.

sections.h2: How does the inspection step work in order?
sections.html:
1. The seller or the seller's agent files the application with the Division of Housing Inspections and pays the fee.
  2. The owner authorizes access, since the buyer cannot enter the house before the sale.
  3. The inspector checks zoning, fire safety, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors and general habitability.
  4. The city returns a list of violations, if any.
  5. The owner corrects them and requests a re-inspection, which carries its own fee after the first.
  6. The certificate is issued and stays good for six months, so closing needs to fall inside that window.

If the sale slips past six months, plan for a new inspection. A buyer who has agreed to handle the certificate takes this over, so spell out who is responsible in the contract.

Trenton bills quarterly, with payments due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1 and a 10-day grace period. Interest runs at 8% a year on delinquencies up to $1,500 and 18% above that, and a 6% penalty can apply to a delinquency over $10,000 left unpaid at year end. Bills go out twice a year, in late June or early July for the August and November quarters and in late December or early January for February and May.

Appeals of a regular assessment are due by April 1 each year, and appeals of added or omitted assessments by December 1. Forms come from the Tax Assessor or the County Tax Administrator.

Any municipal charge unpaid on May 11 of the fiscal year can go to tax sale before June 30. Trenton Water Works has also announced that eligible unpaid water and sewer balances can be certified to the tax sale. When a house sells, the tax bill goes to the new owner, and the seller's closing statement should show the quarter that was paid.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes or a failed inspection
sections.html:
Two problems turn up often with older Trenton houses: back taxes and a failed housing inspection. Both can be handled in a sale.

  • Ask the Tax Assessor or collector for the amount owed, including any water and sewer balance.
  • Ask the Division of Housing Inspections for the list of violations and whether a re-inspection fee applies.
  • Decide with your attorney whether to repair, price the work into a cash offer, or use the unoccupied-until-certified affidavit.

Interest on a delinquency builds at 8% a year up to $1,500 and 18% above that, so a long delay adds up. An owner who inherited a house and cannot afford the repair has a real reason to look at a cash sale.

Trenton is the only New Jersey city served by Amtrak, NJ Transit and SEPTA. The Trenton Transit Center is the end of the Northeast Corridor line to New York Penn Station and of SEPTA's line to Philadelphia, and the River Line light rail runs to Camden. State employment keeps weekday demand steady, with roughly 20,000 state workers commuting in each day.

faqs.q: Does a Trenton house have to pass inspection to sell?
faqs.a: Yes, a residential transfer needs a Certificate of Housing Code Compliance, or an affidavit that nobody will occupy the house until one is obtained. The base fee is $200, and the certificate lasts six months.

faqs.q: Can a buyer apply for the Trenton certificate instead of the seller?
faqs.a: A buyer can apply only when the buyer is the one responsible for obtaining it, because the buyer has no legal right to the property before the sale. Otherwise the seller or the seller's agent files, authorizes access and pays the fee.

faqs.q: What happens if my Trenton house fails the inspection?
faqs.a: The city gives the seller a list of violations, and the certificate is issued after they are fixed. Re-inspections cost $50 each after the first for one or two units, and $25 per unit for larger buildings.

faqs.q: What are the Trenton tax due dates?
faqs.a: Taxes are due on the first of February, May, August and November, with a 10-day grace period before interest starts. Interest is 8% on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18% above it.

faqs.q: Do I need a landlord license to sell a rental in Trenton?
faqs.a: Owners who rent out property need a yearly license under the Absentee Owner Program, renewed in January. Call the Division of Housing Inspections to confirm the license is current before listing or accepting an offer.
